research_text:
## 1. API and finding

`java.security.KeyFactory` converts between opaque public or private `Key` objects and transparent `KeySpec` representations of their key material. It can also translate between compatible specifications of the same key. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

For the supplied rule, “no construction of the key spec was observed” concerns the **`KeySpec` value passed to `generatePublic(keySpec)` or `generatePrivate(keySpec)`**. The rule requires the abstract predicate `speccedKey[keySpec, _]`. It does **not** itself define how that predicate is established, so the message alone does not establish that a valid specification was never constructed or that its key material is invalid. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyFactory.crysl))

## 2. Documented usage and remediation

Oracle documents obtaining a factory for the key’s algorithm, then supplying a compatible public or private key specification to the corresponding generation method. An inappropriate specification causes `InvalidKeySpecException`; requesting an algorithm unavailable from the relevant provider causes `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

Oracle’s example constructs an `X509EncodedKeySpec` from an encoded DSA public key and passes it to a DSA factory’s `generatePublic`. The specification constructors assume the bytes have the stated encoding; construction alone is not documented as establishing the key’s authenticity or suitability for a particular security purpose. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

The reviewed Oracle API documentation does **not** prescribe a detector-specific remediation for this finding. Its documented API correction for an inappropriate input is to provide an appropriate specification for the factory and operation. Whether that also satisfies this analyzer’s predicate cannot be determined from the rule file alone. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- `X509EncodedKeySpec` represents an X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` public key; `PKCS8EncodedKeySpec` represents a PKCS #8 private-key encoding. These descriptions do not guarantee that an arbitrary existing persisted or wire format is interchangeable with either format. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))
- Oracle documents conversion between **compatible** key specifications using a key factory. It does not document a general migration path for changing algorithms or for every stored or transmitted format. Compatibility depends on the actual algorithm, encoding, provider and consumers. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))
- Platform support varies. Java 8 requires `DiffieHellman`, `DSA` and `RSA` factories; the Java 26 API additionally lists `EC`, `RSASSA-PSS` and `X25519` among required factories. Other algorithms depend on the implementation and provider. Standard names include algorithms outside the rule’s five-name list, and standard names are case-insensitive; the rule file does not explain how its analyzer implements string comparison. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/KeyFactory.html?utm_source=openai))

## 4. Exact rule in the supplied source

The source’s specification and event clauses are: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyFactory.crysl))

```text
SPEC java.security.KeyFactory
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
gpr1: privateKey = generatePrivate(keySpec);
gpu1: publicKey = generatePublic(keySpec);
```

The file groups the two `getInstance` events as `Get` and orders a `Get` before zero or more generation events. The event declarations **do constrain the written parameter lists**: one or two arguments for `getInstance`, and one `keySpec` argument for each generation method. The second `getInstance` argument is written as `_`; the file gives it no further constraint. It declares `algorithm` as `String` and `keySpec` as `java.security.spec.KeySpec`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyFactory.crysl))

The rule lists `RSA`, `DiffieHellman`, `DH`, `DSA` and `EC` in its algorithm constraint, and requires `speccedKey[keySpec, _]`. The file does not define that predicate’s provenance or validation strength. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyFactory.crysl))

**A shared method name alone is not what the rule text specifies:** it declares `java.security.KeyFactory` and the argument patterns above. However, the file itself does not specify the analyzer’s method-resolution or receiver-matching implementation. Therefore, from this source alone, it is not possible to categorically rule out an implementation matching an unrelated same-name method. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyFactory.crysl))

## Source limits

- Rule source, on the mutable `master` branch: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyFactory.crysl. The supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified.
- Oracle `KeyFactory` API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html
- Oracle standard names: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- Encoding specifications: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/PKCS8EncodedKeySpec.html

The actual analyzer version, target runtime and provider, key-spec provenance, and persisted or wire formats remain unspecified.
